pairs.rationale: Both salutations name Paul as Christ Jesus' apostle through God's will and address God's Church in Corinth. The brother named with him differs: Timothy here, Sosthenes there. The associated saints/readers are described differently, so this is a formal greeting correspondence rather than one identical recipient list.

The grace-and-peace greeting from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ matches the earlier Corinthian greeting. It is the same salutation formula in two distinct letters, not an additional event or a second completion of the earlier source verse.

Both bless the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and speak of mercy. Corinthians calls Him Father of mercies and God of comfort; Peter's letter describes new birth into living hope through Jesus' resurrection. Their opening praise corresponds while the following benefits differ.

The later account gives concrete comfort received from God through Titus' arrival and the comfort Titus received because of the Corinthians. That illustrates mediated comfort amid affliction, while this verse states the broader purpose of enabling recipients to comfort others. The scopes and actions remain distinct.

Philippians names fellowship in Christ's sufferings together with knowing His resurrection's power. That corresponds to the participation in Christ's sufferings here; the abounding comfort through Christ is Corinthians' own additional statement, not a verbatim Philippians clause or an identical suffering episode.

Both connect ministerial endurance with other people's salvation. The speaker in2Timothy endures everything for the chosen ones; Corinthians describes affliction and comfort benefiting its readers as they endure. The chosen-ones wording, eternal glory and comfort are not collapsed into the same list.

Both pair participation in suffering with an encouraging prospect. Corinthians confidently pairs shared suffering and shared comfort; Peter's letter urges those sharing Christ's sufferings to rejoice toward His glory's revelation. Present comfort and that future rejoicing retain their distinct expressions.

The later affliction/perplexity/persecution/striking contrasts provide another specific portrait of ministry under severe pressure. Here the Asia experience exceeds their strength and brings despair of living; there it is qualified by not abandoned or destroyed. The link identifies no particular incident and does not erase the earlier despair.

Both explicitly connect trust with God's power to give life to the dead. Corinthians contrasts reliance on self with that God amid a death sentence; Romans describes the God Abraham believed and adds calling things that are not as though they are. The situations and additional claims differ.

Both join remembered rescue with confidence in future deliverance. The2Timothy speaker recalls rescue from a lion's mouth and expects rescue from every evil work and salvation into the heavenly kingdom; Corinthians speaks of deliverance from great death and renewed hope. The lion image, dangers and future wording are not made one identical event.

Romans asks its readers to struggle together in prayers for the writer's rescue and acceptable service. That corresponds to helping through prayer here; the many-person thanksgiving for the granted gift is Corinthians' stated result, not an extra clause in Romans' Judea/Jerusalem requests.

Both defend the integrity of conduct or proclamation before God. Corinthians appeals to conscience, simplicity, sincerity and grace rather than fleshly wisdom; Thessalonians rejects error, deceit, flattery and greed while invoking God's witness. Their particular claims are compared without supplying one identical accusation.

The hope for full understanding is followed by recognition in part and mutual boasting in the Lord Jesus' day. This is an internal continuation of the recognition argument, retaining partial recognition and the hoped-for fullness rather than claiming every reader already understands fully or defining a general interpretation rule.

Both describe the readers as a ground of boasting in relation to the Lord Jesus' day or coming. Corinthians makes the boasting reciprocal; Thessalonians calls its readers the writers' hope, joy and crown of boasting. The reciprocity and particular metaphors are not inserted into the other text.

The following verse spells out the intended visits before and after Macedonia and onward departure to Judea. It gives concrete itinerary content for this stated intention and second grace, without redefining the grace phrase or treating a proposed visit as an independently recorded completed event.

Both plans involve Macedonia and visiting the Corinthians, but their routes differ. Here the intended sequence includes visits before and after Macedonia and onward to Judea; the earlier letter says Macedonia first, then a hoped-for stay. No identical finalized itinerary or travel date is imposed.

Both use the yes-yes/no-no formulation. Matthew gives the alternatives for plain speech; Corinthians asks whether the planning charge would mean both yes and no in the writer. The shared words serve different rhetorical purposes, rather than one identical quoted instruction or a completed admission of fickleness.

The earlier letter explicitly says God is faithful in connection with calling into His Son's fellowship. That same divine-faithfulness declaration grounds the rejection of contradictory yes/no proclamation here; the calling and message-reliability applications remain distinct.

The earlier arrival-and-proclamation account places Jesus Christ crucified at the center of what the writer knew among the readers. This corresponds to the Christ-centered proclamation recalled here; the named coworkers, Son-of-God title and yes emphasis are this verse's additional details.

Acts announces fulfillment of the promise to the fathers by raising up Jesus and cites the second psalm. Corinthians affirms God's promises as yes in Christ and adds the through-Him Amen to God. The particular fulfilled promise illustrates the connection without reducing all promises to that one narrated proclamation.

Both use anointing language for divine provision. Corinthians names God establishing the writers with the readers in Christ and anointing them; John says the readers have an anointing from the Holy One and all of them know. The agents' titles, recipients and associated benefits retain their actual forms.

Both join sealing with the Spirit as pledge. Corinthians places that pledge in the hearts; Ephesians describes hearing, believing, the promised Holy Spirit and the pledge of inheritance toward redemption. The repeated images correspond while their stated sequence and additional objects are not made identical.

The following decision not to come again in sorrow supplies a direct internal counterpart to not returning to Corinth in order to spare the readers. The God-as-witness declaration belongs here; the linked decision does not independently supply an extra visit, date or outside witness.

Both distinguish ministry from lording it over those served. Corinthians calls the writers fellow workers for joy and says the readers stand in faith; Peter's letter instructs elders to shepherd willingly and become examples. Their offices, images and additional motives remain particular to each passage.

The later purpose for writing while absent is to avoid acting sharply when present and to build up rather than pull down. It provides another specific visit-policy comparison for avoiding a return in sorrow; no extra visit chronology or identical moment is reconstructed.

The next verse's writing to avoid grief from those who should give joy develops this reciprocal sorrow/joy question. This is an internal explanation of the pastoral problem, not an independent account that identifies a particular missing letter or an unnamed person's history.

Both discuss writing, sorrow and an outcome of joy. Here the writer seeks a visit without grief and speaks of shared joy; later he rejoices that letter-caused sorrow led to repentance. The passages do not independently establish which writings or occasions are identical.

Both explain personally costly ministry through affection for the recipients. Corinthians describes tears and anguish in writing so the readers know abundant love; Thessalonians describes longing and sharing not only the gospel but their own lives because the readers became beloved. The actions and settings differ.

The earlier Corinthian discipline passage contrasts being puffed up with communal mourning in response to a particular wrong. It supplies a comparison for an individual's effect on the community, while this verse qualifies sorrow as reaching all in part. The unnamed sorrow-causer is not identified as that earlier offender.

The sufficient-punishment judgment is followed by forgiveness, comfort and confirmation of love for the person. This direct internal conclusion-and-response connection explains the move toward restoration, without assigning an unprinted offense or claiming punishment should continue indefinitely.

Both direct a restorative response toward a person after wrongdoing. Corinthians emphasizes forgiveness and comfort against excessive sorrow; Galatians instructs gentle restoration and warns the restorers about their own temptation. The particular risks, community and unlisted offense are not made identical.

The preceding forgiveness-and-comfort command identifies the practical response and excessive-sorrow risk behind confirming love toward him. This is an internal referent/action connection; it neither supplies the person's name nor treats the appeal as a separate historical incident.

The later account reports Titus remembering the obedience of all the readers in receiving him. That is a concrete internal obedience comparison for the purpose of testing obedience here. Obedient in everything and obedience of you all have different scopes, and the link does not identify every writing mentioned as one letter.

Both describe interpersonal forgiveness in relation to the Lord or Christ. Corinthians joins the readers' forgiveness with the writer's, for their sake in Christ's presence; Colossians commands mutual forgiveness patterned on the Lord's forgiveness. The forgiving agents, conditions and rationale remain distinct.

Both connect communal conduct with denying hostile spiritual advantage. Corinthians names Satan's designs in the forgiveness discussion; Ephesians prohibits sinful or prolonged anger and giving a place to the devil. The particular conduct and advantage/place imagery are related rather than one identical incident.

Both describe an opened door in a proclamation itinerary. This verse places it at Troas in the Lord; the earlier letter names Ephesus, a great effective door and many opponents. The shared opportunity image does not make the cities, circumstances or itineraries identical.

The later account resumes Macedonia, lack of rest and Titus' arrival bringing comfort. It is a concrete internal narrative connection to leaving after not finding Titus here. My spirit and our flesh, Titus' absence and arrival, and the stated stages remain distinct rather than being merged into one simultaneous scene.

Both use the image of leading in triumph. Corinthians thanks God for leading us in triumph in Christ; Colossians describes stripped rulers and authorities displayed and led in triumph in it after its cross statement. The participants and in-Christ/in-it wording differ; no unprinted procession ritual is supplied.

Both direct fragrance imagery toward God with Christ named. Corinthians calls the ministers Christ's fragrance among saved and perishing people; Ephesians calls Christ's self-giving an offering and sacrifice for a fragrant aroma. The shared image does not make the ministers' activity the identical offering described of Christ.

The saved/perishing contrast from the preceding fragrance statement corresponds to the cross-word being God's power to those being saved and foolishness to those perishing. The life/death aromas and power/foolishness descriptions differ, and the sufficiency question belongs to this verse rather than the selected earlier statement.

Both defend a divinely entrusted message against corrupt motives. Corinthians contrasts peddling God's word with sincerity and speaking from God in Christ; Thessalonians denies deceit, flattery and a pretext for greed while speaking before God. Their charges and commissions are related, not one identical misconduct report.

A concrete example of a recommendation letter appears when brothers write to disciples to receive Apollos. Corinthians asks whether such letters to or from the recipients are needed; Acts does not describe a recommendation letter for Paul in this exchange.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: The next description develops the community-as-letter image: a letter of Christ produced through ministry, written by the Spirit rather than ink. Our letter and a letter of Christ remain distinct expressions, and the hearts imagery is not converted into literal paper correspondence.

The contrast of stone with hearts of flesh and the Spirit's work corresponds to God's promise to replace a stony heart with a fleshly heart and put His Spirit within the people. Ezekiel does not use the letter-of-Christ image or name this ministry.

Confidence toward God through Christ corresponds to the bold access in confidence through faith in Him described in Ephesians. The immediate context names Christ Jesus; the comparison does not supply every later claim about ministerial sufficiency.

Sufficiency coming from God rather than ourselves corresponds to Paul's account of labor that is not simply I but God's grace with him. The earlier grace-and-labor statement gives a concrete ministry counterpart without using the same sufficiency vocabulary.

Both explicitly say the Spirit gives life. Corinthians contrasts Spirit with letter in new-covenant ministry; John contrasts the life-giving Spirit with flesh and speaks of Jesus' words. The different contrasting terms are not made interchangeable.

Exodus names Aaron and all Israel's elders as afraid to approach Moses, whose face had been glorified. Corinthians speaks of the sons of Israel unable to gaze at his face and adds the glory being brought to an end. These participants and qualifications are kept as supplied.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: How much more compares the Spirit's ministry with the preceding ministry of death on stones that nevertheless came in glory. The target supplies the explicit lesser-to-greater argument's stated comparison.

The contrast between condemnation and righteousness relates to no condemnation in Christ Jesus and the law's righteous requirement fulfilled in those walking according to the Spirit. Romans develops this through God's action in His Son; it does not repeat the ministry-of-glory formulation.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: The preceding much-more comparison of the ministries' glory explains why the former glory is now described as surpassed. This is the expressed internal comparison rather than a physical measurement of brightness.

What is brought to an end versus what remains relates to Hebrews calling the first covenant old when speaking of a new one, and describing what is growing old as near disappearing. The different wording is preserved without calculating an unprinted date.

The use of great boldness corresponds to the request for bold speech in making known the gospel mystery. Ephesians adds prayer, ambassadorship and being bound by a chain; Corinthians grounds its boldness in the hope just described.

Exodus supplies the actual veil narrative: Moses covers his face after speaking and removes the veil before the Lord. Corinthians states its own purpose concerning the end of what is brought to an end; that purpose is not silently inserted into Exodus.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: Both combine veiling with a barrier to understanding. Here hardened minds and old-covenant reading are discussed; later the gospel is veiled among the perishing and unbelieving minds are blinded. The different objects and stated agents are preserved.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: The notice of Moses being read continues the preceding old-covenant-reading and veil image. The earlier unit supplies the reading setting and unveiling in Christ; here the veil lies over their heart, while the earlier unit speaks of hardened minds.

Moses' removal of the veil on entering before the Lord provides a specific narrative comparison for the veil's removal when one turns to the Lord. Corinthians generalizes the turning statement; the personal action and wider application remain distinct.

Both speak of freedom in relation to the Lord. Corinthians names freedom where the Spirit of the Lord is; Galatians says Christ set the recipients free and warns against a slavery yoke. Neither sentence is rewritten with the other's formulation.

Transformation into the same image while beholding the Lord's glory relates to conformity to the image of God's Son. Romans places this within foreknowledge and predestination; Corinthians describes transformation from glory to glory as from the Lord, the Spirit.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: The same refusal to lose heart recurs later in the argument. Here it follows receiving mercy and ministry; later it stands alongside outward wasting and inward renewal. These are linked reasons for perseverance, not separate claimed events.

Both reject deceitful ministry presentation before God. Thessalonians denies error, uncleanness, deceit, flattering speech and a cover for greed; Corinthians rejects cunning and tampering with God's word in favor of making truth known. Their full descriptions remain distinct.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: The veiled-gospel statement recalls the earlier old-covenant-reading veil. One describes those perishing and the other hardened minds and unveiling in Christ; the related image does not make the passages' audiences or objects identical.

Christ as God's image corresponds to the beloved Son described as the image of the invisible God. Colossians includes deliverance, redemption and forgiveness; it does not repeat the god-of-this-age blinding statement.

Both make Christ the object of proclamation. The earlier statement names Christ crucified and the hearers' differing reactions; this statement names Jesus Christ as Lord and distinguishes the speakers' service from proclaiming themselves.

The God who calls light out of darkness is compared with the creation scene of darkness and God's command for light. Corinthians applies the illumination to hearts and knowledge of God's glory in Jesus Christ's face; Genesis does not state those later clauses or use the identical quotation form.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: The treasure in clay jars makes the surpassing power God's rather than the speakers'. The later answer that power is made complete in weakness gives a specific ministry counterpart to divine power working through human fragility.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: Affliction and distress recur in the commendation of God's ministers through endurance and hardships. This relates the letter's ministry descriptions while preserving the present not-confined and not-utterly-at-a-loss qualifications.

The later defense account distinguishes abandonment by people from the Lord standing with and strengthening the speaker. It provides a particular comparison for support amid persecution, without identifying this general struck-down/not-destroyed ministry portrait as that hearing.

Carrying Jesus' dying so that His life is revealed in the body corresponds to being crucified with Christ and Christ living in the speaker. Galatians also describes life in flesh through faith in God's Son; the different formulations are retained.

Both portray the faithful exposed to death for the Lord's sake. Romans quotes being put to death all day and reckoned as slaughter sheep; Corinthians says living ministers are handed over for Jesus' sake so His life is revealed in mortal flesh. The images and stated purposes differ.

Death at work in the speakers but life in the recipients relates to suffering for the recipients and for the Church as Christ's body. Colossians uses its own affliction description; the comparison concerns ministry suffering benefiting others without equating every clause.

The I-believed-therefore-I-spoke saying is quoted from this Greek-numbered Psalm. Corinthians applies the belief-and-speaking pattern to the speakers; the Psalm's further account of humiliation is not thereby repeated in full.

Both connect God's raising Jesus with life promised to His people. Romans specifically names the indwelling Spirit and giving life to mortal bodies; Corinthians says God will raise us with Jesus and present us together with you. With Jesus is preserved as supplied.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: Both connect benefit reaching others with thanksgiving to God. Here grace increasing through many causes thanksgiving to abound; later generosity and ministry supplying the saints' lack overflow in thanksgivings. The different immediate ministry settings remain distinct.

The inward person's renewal amid outward wasting relates to the prayer for strengthening through God's Spirit in the inner person. Ephesians names divine glory and power without repeating the outer-person decline or daily-renewal wording.

Both contrast present suffering with coming glory. Corinthians calls the affliction momentary and its resulting glory eternally weighty; Romans says present sufferings are not comparable with the glory to be revealed. No calendar or numeric measure is supplied.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: Looking beyond temporary seen things toward eternal unseen things corresponds to walking by faith rather than sight. The later short statement continues the argument's orientation without declaring that every unseen object is automatically eternal.

Both use a tent for the speaker's present bodily existence and envisage its removal. Peter speaks of putting off his tent soon; Corinthians contrasts the dismantled earthly tent with an eternal building from God. Peter does not repeat that complete building description.

Both describe groaning while longing for a future bodily fulfillment. Romans names adoption and the body's redemption; Corinthians uses being clothed over with a heavenly dwelling. Their metaphors are related without making their wording identical.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: The next explanation develops the unclothed/clothed-over image and the desire for mortality to be swallowed by life. It helps locate the present nakedness qualification within that image without replacing even-after-being-unclothed with a different textual reading or supplying an intermediate-body scheme.

Both combine clothing imagery with mortality's transformation. The earlier letter says mortality puts on immortality and death is swallowed in victory; this letter wants to be clothed over so mortality is swallowed by life. The differing objects and phrases remain exact.

Both identify the Spirit as a pledge connected with God's promised future. Ephesians names the promised Holy Spirit as the inheritance pledge; Corinthians says God prepared the speakers for this very thing and gave the Spirit's pledge in its bodily-life argument.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: The later preference reverses the stated home/away contrast: at home in the body and away from the Lord here, away from the body and at home with the Lord there. This is the paragraph's own paired formulation, without mapping an unprinted spatial route.

Walking by faith rather than sight relates to Hebrews' description of faith as assurance of things hoped for and conviction of realities not seen. Hebrews supplies a description of faith; Corinthians applies the contrast within confidence, bodily life and being with the Lord.

The preference to be away from the body and at home with the Lord corresponds to the desire to depart and be with Christ as far better. These express related preferences without independently specifying every intervening event or timetable.

Both make pleasing God or the Lord a goal of conduct. Thessalonians recalls instruction in walking to please God and urges further progress; Corinthians states the aim of being pleasing to Him whether at home or away.

Both bring all the addressed people before a judgment seat and emphasize personal accountability. Corinthians explicitly says Christ's judgment seat and deeds through the body; Romans says God's judgment seat and giving account to God. The different titles are not normalized.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: The hope of being revealed in the recipients' consciences corresponds to commending the speakers to every human conscience before God by making truth known. Both place ministerial credibility before God and human conscience, with the present verse also naming fear and persuasion.

pairs.relationship: internal explanation, contrast or repeated argument
pairs.rationale: The denial of commending ourselves again returns to the earlier question about beginning to commend ourselves and needing recommendation letters. Here Paul gives an occasion to answer appearance-based boasting; the earlier question is not a statement about those opponents' unstated identities.

Both set a charge or description of being beside oneself against sound-minded speech or action. Acts records Festus accusing Paul of madness and Paul asserting truth and sound judgment; Corinthians distinguishes its rhetorical alternatives by service to God or the recipients.

Christ's love and death for others correspond to God's Son loving the speaker and giving Himself for him, alongside being crucified with Christ. Corinthians says One died for all and therefore all died; Galatians's personal me statement does not replace that broader wording.

Both connect Christ's death and life with people living for Him rather than themselves. Romans speaks of living and dying to the Lord and Christ as Lord of dead and living; Corinthians states the purpose that those who live no longer live for themselves.

Both reject a flesh-based criterion of evaluation. John speaks of judging according to the flesh; Corinthians speaks of no longer knowing people or Christ according to the flesh. Knowing and judging remain different stated activities, without denying Christ's actual embodied life.

Both explicitly speak of a new creation in relation to Christ. Galatians contrasts it with circumcision and uncircumcision; Corinthians contrasts old things passing with new things coming to be. No identical list of external practices is supplied.

Both attribute reconciliation to God's action through Christ. Romans describes enemies reconciled through the Son's death and salvation in His life; Corinthians also names the ministry of reconciliation entrusted to the speakers.

Not counting the world's trespasses against them has a specific counterpart in the blessing of the person to whom the Lord does not count sin. The world/community wording and individual blessing are distinguished; the target does not itself narrate entrusting the reconciliation word.

Both use ambassador language for gospel service. Ephesians identifies a speaker as an ambassador bound by a chain who seeks bold speech; Corinthians describes the speakers appealing on Christ's behalf for reconciliation. The imprisonment statement is specific to Ephesians.

Christ's sinlessness and His acting for others' righteousness correspond to the One who committed no sin bearing our sins in His body so that we might live to righteousness. Peter's bearing-sins wording and Corinthians' made-to-be-sin wording remain distinct rather than being silently paraphrased as the same clause.
